title: CI with GitHub Actions
intro: Continuous integration (CI) automatically builds and tests your application whenever changes are pushed or proposed. In this lesson, you will learn how GitHub Actions workflows are structured, how to run Java and React checks in parallel, how matrices and caching work, and how a successful workflow can become a required gate before code is merged.
body:
## What CI is

**Continuous integration (CI)** is the practice of automatically validating code changes as they enter a shared repository. Instead of relying on every developer to remember every test and build command, the CI system runs those checks consistently.

For the full-stack application from the previous lessons, a useful CI pipeline might look like this:

~~~text
Pull request
     |
     v
Checkout source
     |
     +-------------------+
     |                   |
     v                   v
Backend tests        Frontend tests
     |                   |
     +---------+---------+
               |
               v
          Build images
               |
               v
       Publish to GHCR
~~~

CI does not mean that every deployment is automatic. A CI workflow can simply verify that the code is healthy. Later, a separate continuous delivery or deployment stage can take a validated artifact and deploy it.

The main goal is fast feedback. If a developer introduces a compilation error or breaks a test, the team should discover it before the change reaches the main branch.

---

## GitHub Actions workflows

GitHub Actions stores workflow files under:

~~~diagram
{"type": "tree", "title": "Anatomy of a workflow", "root": {"label": ".github/workflows/ci.yml", "children": [{"label": "on", "sub": "push · pull_request"}, {"label": "jobs", "highlight": true, "children": [{"label": "backend", "sub": "runs-on: ubuntu-latest", "children": [{"label": "steps", "sub": "checkout · setup-java · mvn verify"}]}, {"label": "frontend", "sub": "runs-on: ubuntu-latest", "children": [{"label": "steps", "sub": "checkout · setup-node · npm test"}]}]}]}}
~~~

~~~text
.github/workflows/
~~~

A repository might contain files such as:

~~~text
.github/
└── workflows/
    ├── ci.yml
    └── docker.yml
~~~

A workflow is a YAML document describing when automation runs and what it does.

A minimal workflow looks like this:

~~~yaml
name: CI

on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
  pull_request:
    branches: [main]

jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - run: ./mvnw verify
~~~

The `name` gives the workflow a human-readable name.

The `on` section defines events that trigger it. The `jobs` section defines the work that GitHub should perform.

The exact action versions you use should be reviewed periodically. Pinning or otherwise controlling action versions is an important part of supply-chain security.

---

## Push and pull request triggers

A workflow can run when code is pushed to a branch:

~~~yaml
on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
~~~

It can also run for pull requests targeting a branch:

~~~yaml
on:
  pull_request:
    branches: [main]
~~~

You can combine both:

~~~yaml
on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
  pull_request:
    branches: [main]
~~~

This gives you two useful checks:

- Changes pushed directly to `main` are validated.
- Pull requests targeting `main` are validated before they are merged.

In a team workflow, pull request checks are particularly important because branch protection can require them to pass before merging.

---

## Jobs, runners, and steps

A **job** is a group of steps that runs on a GitHub-hosted or self-hosted runner.

For example:

~~~yaml
jobs:
  backend:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - run: ./mvnw verify
~~~

`runs-on` selects the operating environment. `ubuntu-latest` is a common choice for Java and Node.js projects.

A job contains `steps`. A step can use a reusable GitHub Action or execute a shell command.

For example:

~~~yaml
steps:
  - uses: actions/checkout@v4
  - run: ./mvnw verify
~~~

The first step checks out the repository. The second executes the Maven verification lifecycle.

Jobs are isolated from one another by default. If two jobs need the same source code, each job normally checks it out independently.

---

## Checking out the source code

GitHub-hosted runners start with a clean environment. Your repository therefore needs to be checked out before the workflow can compile or test it.

The standard action is:

~~~yaml
- uses: actions/checkout@v4
~~~

After this step, the repository files are available in the runner's workspace.

You should generally place checkout before steps that need your source code, such as Maven, npm, Docker builds, or scripts stored in the repository.

---

## Setting up Java 21

The backend in this course uses Java 21. GitHub Actions can install and configure the required JDK with `actions/setup-java`.

A useful configuration is:

~~~yaml
- uses: actions/setup-java@v4
  with:
    distribution: temurin
    java-version: '21'
    cache: maven
~~~

The `distribution` specifies the JDK distribution. `java-version` selects Java 21. `cache: maven` enables caching of Maven dependencies between workflow runs where supported.

The cache can make repeated builds considerably faster because dependencies do not have to be downloaded from scratch every time.

You should still expect a clean build environment. A cache is an optimization, not something your build should require for correctness.

---

## Setting up Node.js

The React frontend uses Node.js and npm. GitHub Actions provides `actions/setup-node` for configuring Node.

For example:

~~~yaml
- uses: actions/setup-node@v4
  with:
    node-version: '22'
    cache: npm
~~~

The `cache: npm` setting allows npm's package cache to be reused between compatible workflow runs.

After Node is configured, a reliable CI sequence is:

~~~yaml
- run: npm ci
- run: npm test
- run: npm run build
~~~

`npm ci` installs exactly what is described by the lock file and is designed for automated environments. It is preferable to `npm install` for reproducible CI installations when a lock file is committed.

The tests should run before the production build so that a failing test stops the workflow before later steps waste time.

---

## Running the backend and frontend checks

A complete CI workflow can have separate backend and frontend jobs:

~~~yaml
jobs:
  backend:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-java@v4
        with:
          distribution: temurin
          java-version: '21'
          cache: maven
      - run: ./mvnw verify

  frontend:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: '22'
          cache: npm
      - run: npm ci
        working-directory: frontend
      - run: npm test
        working-directory: frontend
      - run: npm run build
        working-directory: frontend
~~~

The jobs can run in parallel because they do not depend on one another.

Parallel jobs reduce total feedback time. If the backend takes three minutes and the frontend takes two minutes, running them sequentially can take about five minutes. Running them concurrently can bring the critical path closer to three minutes, ignoring runner startup and other overhead.

---

## Job dependencies with needs

Sometimes jobs should not run immediately.

~~~widget ci-pipeline
~~~

Suppose you want to build a Docker image only after both backend and frontend checks pass:

~~~yaml
jobs:
  backend:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - run: ./mvnw verify

  frontend:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - run: npm ci
      - run: npm test
      - run: npm run build

  package:
    needs: [backend, frontend]
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - run: echo "Build images"
~~~

`needs` creates a dependency between jobs.

Without `needs`, GitHub Actions may start the jobs independently. With `needs: [backend, frontend]`, the `package` job waits for both jobs to complete successfully.

This gives you a simple pipeline structure:

~~~text
backend ----+
            |
frontend ---+--> package
~~~

If one required job fails, the dependent job will normally not run.

---

## Matrix builds

A **matrix build** runs the same job with several combinations of configuration values.

For example, you might want to test multiple Java versions or operating systems:

~~~yaml
strategy:
  matrix:
    java: [17, 21]
    os: [ubuntu-latest, windows-latest]
~~~

GitHub creates combinations such as:

~~~text
Java 17 + Ubuntu
Java 17 + Windows
Java 21 + Ubuntu
Java 21 + Windows
~~~

This is useful when your library or application officially supports multiple environments.

However, matrix builds increase CI usage. Do not add combinations simply because the feature exists. Choose versions and operating systems that represent actual support requirements.

You can also use `include` and `exclude` to customize the matrix. For example, you might exclude an unsupported combination or add extra configuration to one particular job.

---

## Secrets and configuration

CI frequently needs credentials: registry tokens, cloud credentials, signing keys, or other sensitive values.

Do not put secrets directly into a workflow file:

~~~yaml
# Do not do this
run: deploy --token=my-real-secret
~~~

GitHub provides repository and environment secrets that can be referenced by workflows.

For example:

~~~yaml
env:
  REGISTRY_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.REGISTRY_TOKEN }}
~~~

The exact permissions and token configuration should follow the principle of least privilege. A workflow should receive only the permissions it actually needs.

Be especially careful with pull requests from forks. Secrets should not be made available to untrusted code simply because a workflow needs them. Authentication and permissions are part of the CI security model, not an afterthought.

---

## Building and pushing a Docker image to GHCR

GitHub provides the **GitHub Container Registry (GHCR)** for storing container images.

A common workflow is:

~~~text
source code
    |
    v
run tests
    |
    v
build Docker image
    |
    v
push image to GHCR
~~~

The workflow can use Docker's official actions for login, metadata, and build/push operations. A simplified conceptual example is:

~~~yaml
permissions:
  contents: read
  packages: write

steps:
  - uses: actions/checkout@v4

  - uses: docker/login-action@v3
    with:
      registry: ghcr.io
      username: ${{ github.actor }}
      password: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}

  - uses: docker/build-push-action@v6
    with:
      context: .
      push: true
      tags: ghcr.io/example/task-api:latest
~~~

The `GITHUB_TOKEN` is a short-lived token provided to the workflow. The workflow must have appropriate package permissions for pushing to GHCR.

In a real project, image tags should usually identify a specific commit, release, or version rather than relying only on `latest`. Immutable or traceable tags make deployments easier to reproduce and debug.

---

## Branch protection and required checks

CI becomes much more valuable when its results are connected to repository rules.

~~~callout tip Make the checks required
**Settings → Branches → Branch protection rules → main**: require a pull request and the `backend` and `frontend` checks. Now nobody — including you on a tired Friday — can merge red code.
~~~

A protected `main` branch can require specific status checks to pass before a pull request is merged.

For example:

~~~text
Required checks:
[x] backend
[x] frontend
[x] package

Merge allowed
~~~

If the frontend test fails:

~~~text
Required checks:
[x] backend
[ ] frontend
[ ] package

Merge blocked
~~~

This turns CI from a helpful notification into an enforceable quality gate.

Branch protection can also require pull request reviews and prevent force pushes depending on the repository's configuration.

The important principle is that the protected branch should represent code that has passed the checks the team considers essential.

---

## Reading failed workflow logs

A failed workflow is not automatically a CI problem. Often the CI system correctly detected a problem in the application.

Start by finding the first meaningful failure rather than reading every line from the beginning.

For a Maven failure, look for messages such as:

~~~text
[ERROR] Tests run: 12, Failures: 1
~~~

For npm:

~~~text
npm ERR! Test failed
~~~

For a Docker build:

~~~text
ERROR [build 4/6] RUN ./mvnw package
~~~

Then identify:

1. Which job failed?
2. Which step failed?
3. What command was running?
4. What is the first useful error message?
5. Does the failure reproduce locally?

If the same command fails locally, fix the application or test. If it only fails in CI, investigate environment differences such as Java or Node versions, missing environment variables, filesystem assumptions, network access, permissions, or operating system differences.

Do not immediately add retries to every failing step. Retries can hide genuine problems. Use them only where transient failures are expected and the retry has a clear justification.

---

## Caching without hiding problems

Caching is one of the easiest ways to make CI faster, but it should remain an optimization.

Maven dependency caching can reduce repeated downloads:

~~~yaml
- uses: actions/setup-java@v4
  with:
    distribution: temurin
    java-version: '21'
    cache: maven
~~~

Node dependency caching works similarly:

~~~yaml
- uses: actions/setup-node@v4
  with:
    node-version: '22'
    cache: npm
~~~

A correctly configured cache should not change whether the application is correct. If deleting the cache makes the build fail, the build likely depends on something that was not explicitly declared.

CI should remain reproducible from a clean environment.

---

## A practical CI workflow for the course project

For the React + Spring Boot task manager or webshop, a sensible progression is:

~~~text
Pull request
     |
     +------------------+
     |                  |
     v                  v
Backend verify      Frontend test/build
     |                  |
     +--------+---------+
              |
              v
       Docker image build
              |
              v
         GHCR push
~~~

The first goal should be reliable tests and builds. Once those are stable, add Docker image creation. After that, publishing to GHCR becomes useful because another deployment system can pull a known image.

Avoid building a huge workflow immediately. A small CI pipeline that developers trust is more valuable than a complicated pipeline that frequently produces unexplained failures.

---

## Common mistakes

### Running only tests but not the production build

A test suite can pass while the production frontend build or Docker image fails. CI should eventually validate the artifacts you intend to ship.

### Using npm install in CI

When a lock file is committed, `npm ci` provides a more reproducible installation for automated environments.

### Putting all jobs into one giant job

Separate backend and frontend jobs can run in parallel and make failures easier to understand.

### Forgetting job dependencies

If packaging requires successful backend and frontend checks, use `needs` rather than assuming GitHub will execute jobs in the desired order.

### Hard-coding secrets

Credentials belong in GitHub's secret or environment mechanisms, not in committed YAML files.

### Giving workflows excessive permissions

Use the smallest permissions necessary. For example, a workflow that only reads source code does not need package publishing permissions.

### Treating every failure as flaky

Read the first meaningful error and reproduce it locally when possible. Blindly adding retries makes debugging harder and can allow real defects to remain hidden.

### Using only the latest image tag

A deployment tied only to `latest` can be difficult to trace back to the source commit. Prefer tags that make the exact artifact identifiable.

---

## What CI gives you

GitHub Actions turns your repository into an automated validation system. A pull request can automatically compile Java, run backend tests, install frontend dependencies, run frontend tests, create production builds, and eventually produce Docker images.

The most important part is not the YAML syntax. It is the engineering workflow behind it:

~~~text
change code
   -> validate automatically
   -> get fast feedback
   -> fix failures
   -> merge only when required checks pass
   -> create a traceable artifact
~~~

Once this process is reliable, deployment becomes much safer. You know that the code being packaged has passed the checks defined by the project, and you can connect the resulting Docker image to a release or deployment process.

CI is therefore the bridge between development and delivery: it turns a Git commit into evidence that the software can be built and tested consistently.
takeaways: GitHub Actions workflows define automated CI in YAML files under .github/workflows.
Jobs can run independently in parallel, while needs creates explicit dependencies between jobs.
setup-java and setup-node configure the required runtimes and can cache Maven or npm dependencies.
Matrix builds test multiple supported combinations without duplicating the workflow definition.
Secrets and least-privilege permissions are essential when CI accesses registries or deployment systems.
Required branch checks turn CI results into a merge gate and help keep the main branch healthy.

quiz.question: What is the primary purpose of continuous integration?
options: To automatically validate code changes through repeatable builds and tests
To replace version control
To guarantee that every deployment is successful
To run the application only on a developer's computer
quiz.explanation: CI automatically builds and tests changes so the team receives fast, consistent feedback about whether the code is still healthy.

quiz.question: What does `needs: [backend, frontend]` do for a GitHub Actions job?
options: It runs backend and frontend inside the same process
It makes the job wait until both named jobs complete successfully
It disables both jobs
It forces the jobs to run on Windows
quiz.explanation: The needs property creates job dependencies. A job with both backend and frontend in needs waits for those jobs before it can run successfully.

quiz.question: What is a matrix build useful for?
options: Storing passwords in workflow files
Publishing every Docker image automatically
Running the same job across multiple combinations of configuration values
Replacing all Git branches with one branch
quiz.explanation: A matrix lets GitHub Actions expand one job definition into multiple combinations, such as several Java versions and operating systems.

quiz.question: Which command is normally preferred for installing npm dependencies in CI when a lock file is committed?
options: npm init
npm publish
npm update
npm ci
quiz.explanation: npm ci is designed for clean, reproducible automated installations based on the package lock file.

quiz.question: Why should a CI workflow use minimal permissions?
options: To make YAML files shorter
To reduce the potential impact if the workflow or an action is compromised
To make Docker images smaller
To prevent pull requests from running
quiz.explanation: Least-privilege permissions reduce what a compromised workflow can access or modify, limiting the potential impact of a supply-chain or workflow security problem.

exercise.title: Model CI job stages, matrices, and triggers
exercise.task:
Define exactly these three functions:

1. `function jobStages(jobs)` — `jobs` is an object where each value may contain `needs` as a string, an array of strings, or no `needs` property. Return an array of stages, where each stage is an array of job names. Stage 0 contains jobs with no dependencies. Each later stage contains jobs whose dependencies are all present in earlier stages. Sort job names alphabetically within every stage. Throw an `Error` whose message contains `"cycle"` if some jobs can never run because of a dependency cycle. Throw an `Error` whose message contains `"unknown"` if a job depends on a job that does not exist.

2. `function expandMatrix(matrix)` — `matrix` contains ordinary matrix keys such as `java` and `os`, each containing an array of values. It may also contain `include` and `exclude` arrays. Return the cartesian product of the ordinary matrix keys as objects. Preserve the matrix key order, with the first key changing slowest. Remove combinations that match every key of an `exclude` entry, then append every `include` entry as its own combination. `include` and `exclude` must not appear as keys in the returned combinations.

3. `function shouldRun(trigger, event)` — `trigger` can contain event names such as `push` and `pull_request`. Each event configuration may contain a `branches` array. Return `true` when the trigger contains `event.name` and either that configuration has no `branches` list or the event branch matches one of the listed patterns. An exact branch pattern matches only that branch. A pattern ending in `/*` matches any branch starting with the prefix before the `*`, so `release/*` matches `release/1.2`. Return `false` when the event is not configured or no branch pattern matches.

Do not mutate any input objects or arrays.
exercise.hint: For `jobStages`, normalize `needs` to a copied array, validate every dependency first, then repeatedly collect jobs whose remaining dependency sets are empty. Sort each ready group before adding it as a stage. If no job is ready while jobs remain, there is a cycle. For `expandMatrix`, recursively build the cartesian product in key order, then remove combinations where every key in an exclude rule matches, and finally append copied include entries. For `shouldRun`, first find the configuration by event name; a missing branches array means the event is allowed, while a pattern ending in `/*` should compare the branch against the prefix before the `*`.

tests.name: It creates separate job stages from dependencies
It accepts a single string dependency
It alphabetically sorts jobs within the same stage
It creates as many stages as required by dependency depth
It reports a cycle
It reports an unknown dependency
It does not mutate the jobs input
It creates the matrix cartesian product in key order
It excludes matching matrix combinations
It appends include entries without adding include or exclude keys
It runs an event when no branch filter is configured
tests.code: return shouldRun({ push: {} }, { name: "push", branch: "feature/x" }) === true;

tests.name: It matches exact and wildcard branch patterns
It rejects events that are not configured
tests.code: return shouldRun({ push: { branches: ["main"] } }, { name: "pull_request", branch: "main" }) === false;
